utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Considering that you had been to Kosovo six times within a relatively short time, I suppose that you are pretty familiar with the situation there, so I now have a specific question. Did the local population, according to what you know, frequently dig trenches for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about whether they did it as a form of forced labour? Were they forced to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've lost the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk about that with Albanian villagers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't have the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes they dug trenches of their own free will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear on this microphone? Can you hear the English now? "A. Sometimes they dug trenches of their own free will, sometimes they were forced to do so."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about stories or rumours that in Mala Krusa - and that's precisely the area where you were deployed at the critical time - there are over a hundred people? You were there. Did you hear or see anything that would indicate that a crime had been perpetrated there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard or saw anything about a hundred people being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there ever any shooting there that could be linked to such an event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard shooting of such intensity that it could kill such a number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a member of special police units, you were there many times with a lot of your friends, comrades, and you had been in the police for a long time, although you're a young man, do you consider it possible for our police to round up some citizens and take them away to execute them? Can you possibly imagine even the worst policemen in our services do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't imagine anyone that I know doing anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it doesn't matter what the witness could imagine or what you could imagine. What we have to deal with is the evidence, so that sort of question is totally irrelevant. Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if we were dealing only with facts, none of this would be happening. You didn't allow me to quote to Vollebaek Clinton's own speech where Clinton is lying through his teeth about women and children being executed in Racak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you have heard what we've said. Now, there are bounds to what's relevant, and the sort of question of what a witness could imagine or not imagine is wholly irrelevant. It doesn't matter what he could imagine. It's the facts and the evidence with which we are dealing, particularly the evidence. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll stick to facts, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, you would certainly remember if you had seen or heard anything about that, if you had heard shooting or anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any houses burnt down in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps two or three. I can't tell you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were those fires of a large scale?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing on a large scale. I don't know how they were burnt down; from rifle fire or otherwise, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say you didn't see how they were burned. Can you even guess how they were burnt down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please answer me precisely: Did our police, for instance your unit, burn anybody -- burn anybody's house down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did you have occasion to speak to your colleagues about those events? Do you have any knowledge that your colleagues had heard anything about what was talked about, those operations in Mala Krusa, torchings, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody knows anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you there exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 25th to the 27th or 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this specific event took place on the 26th of March. So you were there at the critical time, on the spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From your written statement, I understand that you first heard about this event from investigators of this Tribunal when they interviewed you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I first heard of it actually on the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you heard that news on TV and you had been there previously, what was your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't believe it. And I talked to my colleagues later, and nobody could tell me anything about it. Nobody knew anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you took part in the operations. You had been to Mala Krusa. You hadn't seen any of those vehicles coming to Mala Krusa. You don't know who could have possibly done such a thing, and according to your testimony, the police couldn't have done it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From our company, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it possible that when they were burying some people, that those were actually members of the KLA who had been killed in fighting with our forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's well outside the ability of this witness to deal with. It's entirely speculative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was there. Do you know who was buried? First of all, do you know if anybody was buried, Witness K25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the first I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know about stories concerning alleged planting of hand grenade booby-traps in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were in your positions around Mala Krusa, was there any artillery fire from your positions, such as from cannons, tanks, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you in the PJP use except for your infantry weapons, hand-held Zolja rocket launchers? Did you have any heavier weapons, artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our company didn't, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything at all about removal of dead bodies in Mala Krusa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of it here for the first time. I know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were in Kosovo, did you or your colleagues hear about this event, about such an event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While you were responding to questions in chief yesterday, you said that ribbons were worn, and I understood you as saying that you had a code which told you every day what colours are to be worn, and that prevented the KLA from coming close to the police and playing a dirty trick on them. Do you have any knowledge about the KLA using or, rather, abusing uniforms of our police in order to commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know of one incident in 1998 when they were dressed in our uniforms, and they called out to our colleagues who were standing on the road, and as a result, those people were injured by the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Here in this room we heard about municipal Crisis Staffs and things like that. Have you ever heard anything about that? Did you know about it? And do you know that such staffs were organised within municipalities to deal with their everyday problems during crisis situations and to organise citizens? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday in response to a question of the opposite side, you explained what the task was of the local reservists, and I noted down what you said. You replied, "They protected and defended themselves." Is that in fact the entirety of your answer? Does it mean that there was not enough police there to protect the civilians, that reservists defended their own houses and settlements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because the necessity for them to protect themselves indeed existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what you know, did they have any other task except to protect their own settlements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during examination-in-chief, there was talk about an event where I noted down here robbing of refugees, namely three persons, as you described, had attempted to rob some refugees, and you drove them away. Would you please explain when that happened, what exactly happened, who these people were, and were you at all able to determine any of it? Could you please describe this event.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident happened. Indeed I can't tell you the exact date, but it was during our stay in Mala Krusa. Three policemen -- I suppose they were policemen because they were wearing blue camouflage uniforms and masks on their faces -- they tried to rob refugees, but the commander of our company took a stand in front of them and put on his rank insignia in order to drive them away. However, they cocked their weapons at him, and we had to approach too and support him. We eventually drove them away. They retreated. They got into their own vehicles, which were civilian vehicles, and drove away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Civilian vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Three persons. Why didn't you arrest them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in uniform. I said they were in uniform, although they were using civilian vehicles. That was normal there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you said.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian vehicles were in use down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A policeman, when caught red-handed committing a crime is normally arrested.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were afraid they would open fire at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they actually succeed in robbing anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did they approach and what did they want?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They approached refugees who were moving along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a similar experience anywhere else where you met those predators preying on columns of refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the only time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Nice said something about men, women, and children who were at the railway station of Mala Krusa to the effect that they would never have gotten any water there if you hadn't intervened. Could you please explain, did anyone refuse food, water, or medical aid to those refugees? What was the problem with those refugees? Did anyone forbid them from using water, from having access to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that something like that was not customary. It was normal for them to have everything they needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that railway station, did the police force those people to stay at those railway stations to board trains or were those people who came there of their own free will, wishing to leave the territories affected by combat operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had received an explanation that transport would be organised from the railway station, so they stayed there and waited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you see at or around those railway stations that the police, local or otherwise, was mistreating those citizens, beating anyone, doing anything to hurt those people who were waiting for the trains to come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point there were over 500 refugees at the railway station. They were not guarded by anyone. They were alone there. One policeman was standing on the road in order to protect the children who were crossing the road in order to fetch water. There were no other policemen except those few on the road. They were alone at the railway situation, although they were not transported by trains but by buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That makes no difference, and that was not my question. You say one policeman was on the road, protecting children crossing the road in order to fetch water, from anything that might come up and hurt them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was to protect their safety?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand something you said yesterday. You said there were many refugees there, but I noted down, "Nobody came from Velika or Mala Krusa but from the direction of Celine." Were there refugees from the Krusas or elsewhere, or did I misunderstand this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single refugee came from the direction of Velika or Mala Krusa villages. All the refugees came from the direction of Celine Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. village. I don't know from which villages they were originally, but that's where they came from, not from the Krusas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We often hear it said here that the policemen - meaning our policemen - took away money, valuables, watches, rings, jewellery from people, that our police committed many crimes, robberies, murders, rapes. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I know only about this incident which we thwarted, but that's all I know. At least nothing happened which would involve the people I was with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me one more thing: I understand you have a university degree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have a law degree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a law degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said in your written statement that the commander of all those units was General Obrad Stevanovic and the commander of all Kosovo units was General Sreten Lukic. Have you ever, from either headquarters, either from the commander of special units Stevanovic or from General Lukic received any assignment which would run counter to the law or would constitute a violation of the rules governing police work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Including even discrimination in terms of treatment of the population in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of these events, you tell us you were a corporal, I think.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corporal first class, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive instructions directly from generals in the course of your time as a corporal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about what other policemen may have done or did in the course of the incident that you've described. You, I think, were on the road at the junction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the road, as you've told us, there were tanks, other armed police officers, and other deployments further up the road, also armed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The road itself, from time to time, was filled by -- or not filled by, used by refugees, all walking in the same direction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have -- did you yourself ever go to the houses in the Krusas at the time when the people were leaving the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you ever in any position to hear what was said to them or done to them at the time they left their houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but no one from my company ever entered the village because we had no such orders. We were holding blockade lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The police of which you speak -- I beg your pardon. The police of which you've been asked questions in the most general terms, was it in fact composed of several different components, coming from several different places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. If you mean along our road, then yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The people -- if there were police or other armed units in the villages themselves, if there were, were they from a unit different from yours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one in the villages. Along the road, there was the army of Yugoslavia, our company, and the local police, but there was no police inside the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To your knowledge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire was opened at us, and it is certain that policemen were not shooting at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we look at the map that you've shown, we can see that the area --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just put the map on the ELMO again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at the map that's on the overhead projector, is it right that we can see the area with which we are concerned completely surrounded on three sides by forces of either the army or the police? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you've explained, you were never present at any house when any resident left the house or was told or advised to leave the house, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard something about a Zolja. Just remind us what sort of a weapon a Zolja is, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a hand-held rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does that have some form of guidance mechanism that enables it to seek out its target?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one fired in the course of the operation, to your knowledge, at the Mala Krusa bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at the time it was fired, were there, to your knowledge, people at the Mala Krusa bridge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the bridge. Under the bridge there was activity directed against us, and we could not repel them with a hand-held rocket launcher. And after this one shot fired at them, all activity ceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Consistent with or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Consistent with or inconsistent with casualties being suffered at the bridge as a result of the use of the hand-held rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the bridge, no. Let me repeat: Under the bridge there was this going on. And nobody can say whether there were any casualties or not. All I can say is that there was no more shooting from that area afterwards. But that's only my assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked about crimes committed by police or otherwise. So far as you were aware, if the six people or the three people that you saw taken away and never saw again, if they were killed, is that something for which people should be held to account, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked by the accused --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked by the accused an extensive question about the phrase "mop-up." Just help us, please, with when you first heard the phrase "mop-up" and by whom it was used and in what circumstances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was used all the time, that term. But as I said at the beginning, it was just a phrase, an expression.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was a general suggestion put to you about why it was that the refugees were or were not moving. Help us - it's covered in your materials - just yes or no, were you in fact given accounts of what had happened to them by the refugees when they were in the lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were different stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Staying with the refugees, you've been asked accounts of what happened at the railway station, the number of armed people there and so on. If those refugees had wanted to return along the road from which they had come, would that have been along a road where there were tanks and armed police and indeed the army present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat that question? I'm not sure I understood it. Had they wished to return or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had they wished to return along the road from which they had come, would that have been along a road where there were tanks, armed police, and indeed even the VJ army present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had they wished to return, they had to go back the same way they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that nobody emerged from the village of Mala Krusa itself along the road at the junction where you were. Were there other roads, to your knowledge, from Mala Krusa leading towards other villages or don't you know the geography sufficiently well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was up on the blockade lines. I didn't go in-depth into the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness K25, I have some questions about the six KLA members captured by you and handed over to the local MUP. What is suggested is that they might have been executed by the local MUP members. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood your question, Your Honour. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They might have been executed by local MUP members inside the house after having been handed over?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said that you heard the sound of automatic gunfire after they entered the house. What did you do after you heard this automatic gunfire sound? Did you try to find out what it was about or did you talk with your superior about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Along the whole blockade line, there was shooting going on. There was firing from rifles, and this noise coming from that direction left no doubt because there was shooting all the time. We just thought that somebody was trying to escape, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you do after you had found some bodies inside the house? Did you talk with your superior about that or did you try to find out what it was about afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. Everything took place very quickly, so I don't really remember the order and sequence of events, but I think that straight after that, we left the territory and went to engage in our next operation. So I don't know really what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You did nothing after, even after you had seen those bodies, a lot of bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was sent on to the higher authorities but -- and I wrote a report to my own service. I wrote a report to my own service, but I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May I take it that you or your company allowed them, allowed the local MUPs or some paramilitaries doing some bad things? Not by preventing them from doing some bad things or not by punishing them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K25 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could we prevent them when the orders were that they should give themselves up? How were we supposed to know what they would do? We had orders to hand them over to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness K25, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While arrangements are being made for the next witness to be called, can I simply at this stage explain that I will have an administrative matter to raise later in relation to a witness forthcoming, but I will be assisted if I can put off making that application until as late as possible in the morning when my information will be as complete as it's going to be by the time I have to deal with the issue. I think the Chamber knows what I'm dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But raise it at the end of the morning. We've had the application in relation to Colonel Crosland, and we will grant it. That means he will give evidence with facial distortion and redaction of date of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. The witness I was dealing with was K33 and the particular order that relates to him, and we must probably deal with that order today given that the Court is not going to be available tomorrow and Friday, but I need to have maximum information to make my decision, and I'll therefore deal with that at the end of the morning, if I may. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The next witness is Shyhrete Berisha. Do Your Honours -- do you have the summary? It's just a question. I believe it was distributed before, but I just would like to confirm. No? I have copies here. My apologies. I believe -- I thought it was distributed before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: My name is Shyhrete Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Were you born on 5th December, 1961?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Ms. Berisha, do you remember giving a statement to officers of the Office of the Prosecutor on the 17th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you also remember attending a meeting on the 17th of June, 2002 with a presiding officer of this Tribunal, and at that time you had a copy, in the Albanian language, of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Do you also remember making an addendum of your statement?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And at that time, you confirmed that the contents of your statement are correct and true?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The Prosecution submits the statement of Ms. Shyhrete Berisha into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 252.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: This witness is a survivor of the mass killing by Serb police and paramilitaries in Suva Reka on the 26th of March, 1999. Her husband and four children were amongst those killed. The witness is a female Muslim who lived in Suva Reka with her husband Nexhat Berisha and their four children. They shared the house with the family of Faton Berisha, a nephew of the witness's husband. It is situated across the road from the Suva Reka police station. Can I ask, please, the usher to show the witness the first photo. The photo I'm referring to is located in tab 3, photo 14 of the Suva Reka binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, can you confirm if this is the house where you lived with your husband and four children?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. That is the house where I lived with my husband and four children. On the left side. Whereas on the right side was the nephew of my husband, Faton, with Fatime and his wife two children and his sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: In late 1998, OSCE moved from their former headquarters to the witness's house. OSCE used the witness's part of the house as their headquarters and Faton's part of the house as sleeping. After the OSCE pulled out of Kosovo on 20 March, 1999, there were a lot of movement of Serb police and military. On the following days, the witness saw tanks, Pinzgauers and military vehicles. On 25th March early in the morning, the police knocked on the door and forced the witness's husband Nexhat into the part of the house where the OSCE officers had been. He was severely beaten and the rooms containing OSCE equipment were burglarised. The witness and others were robbed of about 50.000 Deutschmarks. Throughout these events, a large tank was parked outside with its gun barrel pointing direct towards the house. After this assault, the witness and her family moved over to the house of her husband's uncle, Vesel Berisha, approximately 30 metres from the witness's house. At this time, there were 25 people of all ages living in Vesel's house.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness names these persons. On the morning of the 26th of March, 1999, two tanks were situated outside Vesel's house with their gun barrels pointing towards it. At 12.20 p.m., many men, approximately 30 in number, some in police uniforms and some in civilian clothes, all carrying automatic weapons, run over from the police station to the house of the witness. One of these men, known as Zoran, family name perhaps Popovic or similar, from Suva Reka, called for one of the house occupants, Bujar, to come out. And on doing so, Bujar was shot dead. The other occupants were terrified and run out, trying to escape. All the men were stopped. The witness's husband, Nexhat, was told by one named Miskovic to raise his hands in the air. He did so, and the witness saw him shot in the back by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. Romano please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: My apologies. She was holding the hands of two of their children at the time. There was a lot of shooting and many people were wounded. The survivors, 40 or 50 people, mainly women and children with several Berisha families, were forced into a cafe. Can I have the witness shown the second photo. This photo is also located in the Suva Reka binder, Exhibit 166. It's photo number 2, tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, is this the coffee shop where you were?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. This is the coffee shop where the Serb police killed my four children, the children of my sister-in-law, and two other -- the members -- the other members of the Berisha family, of the two Berisha families. They forced us into the cafe and told us to sit down. Some were sitting on blankets and some were sitting on chairs. But very soon after that, they began shooting with automatic weapons. The first one I saw who was closest to me was Zoran, with a lot of others. And after that, I didn't see any more because there were so many people around. And I just heard the shooting, the firing. It lasted about 20 minutes, maybe 30 minutes, without interruption at all. Shooting kept on all the time. Then it stopped, the shooting, and then I looked up and I saw Vjollca was still alive and said, "Oh, Shyhrete, look what they're doing to us." I said, "Look at, look at Dafina, see where she is." And I looked around and I saw Dafina, Vjollca's daughter. She was suffering. And the daughter of Musli Berisha said, "Oh, look what they've done to me. Look at my feet, look at my legs," she screamed. And then the bother-in-law of Hajdini said, "Look at my poor Granit. Look what they've done to him."

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Ms. Berisha --

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Then Majlinda spoke, my largest daughter. She was uninjured, with her son and brothers. And Sebahate was uninjured with her two children. Ismet was 3 and Eron was ten months old. And Altin was near me. He was ten years old. We were uninjured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Berisha, help us with this: How old were your four children who were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My children were Majlinda Berisha, who was 16; Herolinda, who was 14; Altin who was 11; and Redon, who was only 21 months old -- 22 months old. Then Majlinda said, "Mummy, mummy, look at how they've killed Herolinda." And when I looked around, I saw Herolinda over there and saw her, that she was lying on the ground with five or six bullet holes in her flesh. She had been such a beautiful girl. And Sebahate on the other side said, "Look. They've killed -- they've killed her. They've killed Jori [phoen] and Sherine." Sherine was a brother-in-law, and the other one was his brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, how did you survive?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: It was terrible for me. I don't know how to explain it to you. It was -- it was absolutely horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Did you feign death?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I pretended I was dead. And my son Altin and Vjollca, I said to them, "Lie as if you're dead." Because we heard the Serbs talking in their language, saying, "Get the trucks ready and get the bodies out of here as quickly as possible."

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness and two other survivors and the corpses of the dead were then loaded onto a truck which drove off in the direction of Prizren. Two gold chains were removed from around her neck. The witness, although severely wounded, managed to jump off the truck in the village of Malsia e Re (Ljutoglav) where some Albanians took care of her. She was taken to Grejkoc and subsequently Budakova, where she received medical treatment for her wounds. Her husband and four children - two daughters and two sons - were killed in Suva Reka. Can I have the witness just shown the map? This map is also located in the Suva Reka binder, tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, if you can, can you just point out the route from Prizren to -- I'm sorry, from Suva Reka to Prizren and the place where you jumped off the truck. I know that the letters are very small, but if you can.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: It's -- this is it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The witness spent six weeks moving around the area under very difficult conditions until around 10th May, 1999, when she managed to cross the border to Albania by joining a convoy. Before they reached the border, they were stopped in the village of Bukosh where some men and women were taken out of the convoy. They were brought to the school and stripped and robbed of all gold and money. Older men and some of the women were released, but the young men were never seen again. At the border with Albania, they had to hand over at gunpoint all their identification papers. The scenes referred to by the witness are all depicted in the Suva Reka binder volume 1, tab 6, photos 1 to 4; tab 3 photos 14 to 24; photos of the firing range in tab 4; and the map at tab 18. Can I have the witness shown the article in the Newsweek magazine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise or are you aware of any magazine or any article written about what happened to your family?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the article.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: And do you know, how did they get this information?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: I think that the head of the OSCE gave them the information, and all the others in Suva Reka provided information too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Anybody from your family?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes, from Vjollca.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: The article containing an extensive report about what happened in Suva Reka is in tab 2 of the Suva Reka binder. That's all, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you have no questions for this witness, then that will be understood, considering the experiences she went through. But of course if you want to challenge her evidence about how she lost her husband and four children, you can do so, but I suggest for once you try and restrain your questioning and keep it to less than the time which you're allowed, which is three-quarters of an hour, given the circumstances of her evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I will use only one minute. And as for the witness, who obviously lost her husband and children, I have no intention whatsoever to question her. I would only like to ask you to accept as an exhibit the statement of Marjan Krasniqi, your pages, your numbers 03045454 until 03045463. He gave a statement in Tirana on 8th June 1999. I received it. He is a former traffic policeman, and in his statement he explains that this crime had been committed by members of a local criminal group, that the reason was money, that among them were people mentally disturbed, and it was not an intra-ethnic thing. There was an Albanian among those criminals by the name of Rexha Berisha. This statement exists and has been disclosed. I just would like to tender it into evidence. This statement proves, or claims, that this crime had been committed by a criminal group. I will not otherwise question this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can tender the statement. We'll consider whether to admit it as an exhibit. However, if it's going to be suggested that -- just a moment. If it's going to be suggested that this was the work of local criminals, the witness should have the chance to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. deal with it and to give her comments which she may have on it since she was there. Just let me --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I only mentioned some of what is written in a statement of your witness, not my witness. I refer to that. I just tendered it into evidence. You accept into evidence newspapers which Mrs. Romano tendered a moment ago, and you are questioning a statement of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Let us have the statement. It's right that the witness should have the chance to deal with it. Give me the statement. Will you go and get it, please. Would you tell the usher to go and get the statement. Would you give it to the usher, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have the page numbers; is that right? Can the registry confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we have the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution can get a copy?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is right now trying to locate and get a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt that will take a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Probably. I just -- I will just confirm. Yes. It's going to be down as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the sensible thing, I think, would be to take a break now while that's being done, and then we'll deal with it. Mrs. Berisha, there may be just a few more questions you're going to be asked when we've got this statement. It is right that you should have the chance to deal with it. We're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. Could you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statements are coming. And since at that time we cannot find the exact passages that the accused referred to. We have one copy here with us that we are reviewing. In fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's have the copy. Let me have the copy and I can examine the witness on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, we believe that this is the one that the accused is referring to. We have two others, but we believe that this is the one that he's referring to. We have highlighted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the statement of Marjan Krasniqi; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that it's difficult quite to follow what the accused is relying on in that statement, but we don't want to detain the witness here. But on the other hand, she should have a chance of dealing with the particular issues which the accused has raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Berisha, can you help us with this, please: Were you able to identify any of those who were responsible for the killing?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us who they were.

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: They were police who were from the police station of Suhareke. I saw them with my own eyes. From the police station, they went first of all to the use of Ismet Kuci, saw that there was no one there, and came to Vesel Berisha's house. They were policemen. They weren't any bands of people, they were police. Not as the accused said. They were actually policemen and I saw them with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How were you able to recognise them as policemen?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: They were policemen because Sedat, Vjollca's husband, said to my husband, "Look at -- all the policemen of Suhareke are here. And there's policemen we don't even know." And I saw them myself. They were all wearing police uniforms. They were police uniforms with automatic weapons in their hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you know any of them before?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: Yes. Among them I knew one, Zoran, who was wearing a police uniform too. And on his shoulder he had a white insignia. He was a paramilitary, I think, because Zoran didn't used to be a policeman. He was only dressed as a policeman that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who was Zoran? You say he wasn't normally a policeman. What did he do?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: He used to drive the bus. He used to be a bus driver. And he spoke Albanian very well. And there were a lot of policemen there. There were about 30. About 30 came to the house where we, 25 members of our family, were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage green and blue, dark blue, uniforms. They were all the same, with caps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Berisha, what did you know about a man called Miskovic? Was he also a policeman or was he a paramilitary like Zoran?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: No, it seems to me he was the commander of the police, but he was wearing plainclothes. He was wearing black.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not in uniform?

utterances.speaker: SHYHRETE BERISHA
utterances.text: No. Miskovic was wearing black clothes. He wasn't wearing a uniform. But the others, about a hundred, when they surrounded our house, about a hundred of them, there were a few Romany civilians among them apart from Miskovic, who was in plainclothes. His brother, who's guard of the house where the OSCE was, apart from him, all others were all wearing police uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Romano. Do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have right now a copy with me, and the delay was just because we had to redact the address that was in the original statement. So you -- probably Your Honours won't be able to exhibit or use the ones you have, but I have one here that I will produce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: First of all, have you any questions for the witness or can we let her go?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: Your Honour, no. I just wanted to highlight and to direct Your Honours to page 6 of the statement that you have in hand, where it refers to Petrovic, Zoran Petrovic. And the witness, while answering the questions, she made reference of the man being a paramilitary, and that's exactly what it is stated in the -- and as you can see, he has been -- it says that he had been involved with the paramilitary service since 1998. I also would like to inform that we tried to locate any reference of any mentally or mentally ill or disturbed persons that the accused made reference, and we could not locate that in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we've finished with the witness, she can go. We will then decide on what should happen to the statement. Do you have any questions of her?

utterances.speaker: MS. ROMANO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mrs. Berisha, thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. That concludes it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will return the copy which we were given, unredacted, of that statement. The issue is now what should happen to it. The accused applies for it to be exhibited. One possible course is this, it being, of course, an uncross-examined statement, is that it should be simply marked for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's one possibility. I've only had a chance briefly to review the statement, but I can see from one of the passages highlighted that it is by no means favourable to the accused's position. Entirely to the contrary. And he may, therefore, be acting ill-advisedly and in a way that he would not act if properly represented in seeking to lay before the Court for a very narrow purpose that we still cannot tie down a document that is adverse to his cause. I also observe, and unless I'm wrong, I don't know that we've exhibited many or any witness statements of witnesses other than the witness giving evidence, and the status of such an exhibited statement would be hard for us to identify at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be, of course, that the right course should be that this witness is called to give evidence, if the accused wants him to give evidence, by the accused. Now, that is the normal way in which such statements are dealt with. The question is, at the moment, what action should we take, if any, about it? The accused wants to have it exhibited. It may be that a simpler course is to simply to mark it for identification purposes and then, in due course, we could decide what should happen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm happy with that course because that doesn't give it any evidential status. But there's one question only and that is the accused has made reference to mental ill health as being a feature of the people who were present, or one of the people present. We haven't yet located it. Before we forget the issue altogether, if he can identify the passage, so much the better so we can at least see what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what's been said by the Prosecutor. The position is this: That this is a witness statement, of course, of someone who hasn't given evidence. And while it's true that we do admit hearsay in various forms, we do not usually admit witness statements unless there are particular reasons for doing so or the Rule comes within -- or the statement comes within Rule 92 bis with which you will now be familiar. The Prosecution suggests that the -- you may want to consider whether to admit the statement. The proper course would be for you, if you thought right, to call this witness during your own case, in which case, of course, he could give his evidence. But meanwhile, if you want still to have this statement exhibited, we will -- we have in mind to mark it for identification. That means at the moment it is not admitted, but it is noted. Now, what do you want to do? And I should add that a final decision about whether it's to be admitted will be taken in due course towards the end of the trial. Now, what course do you want to follow? Do you want it exhibited or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, you can do whatever you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely emphasise that the statement indicates the fact that we're dealing with criminals, and who else could have killed somebody's children, I ask you, but the worst of criminals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will simply mark it for identification with the next Defence exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the only other thing I would add to that is that when I have reviewed the three statements in full, I will give some thought to whether we should apply to serve him as a 92 bis witness in case there's anything that one way or the other might be of material value to the Chamber. But I'll give thought to that in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Defence Exhibit 23, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution calls as our next witness Colonel John Crosland. Your Honours, you will note that I have provided, just moments ago, a summary of this witness's statements in the usual format that the Court is familiar with receiving. In light of Your Honours' order that the witness be partly bis'd and partly live, I will use this summary and indicate to Your Honours where I am. And if there's any particular paragraph which has got a highlight that the Court wants me to deal with live in addition to the ones I propose, I invite Your Honours to simply direct my attention to proceeding with it in a live fashion. At the moment, I propose to summarise paragraphs 1 through 5, take Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. live 6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 18, 19 -- paragraph 19, I believe, might assist a request from the Court on an earlier occasion to have a live witness concerning Racak on the 15th -- 20, 23, 25, and then deal with 27, which are the SitReps. Should there be anything else that the Court wishes me to either summarise or do live, I would be grateful if you would let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The topics which must be dealt with live are the cooperation between the VJ and the MUP and the meetings with the VJ hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Thank you. In light of the very limited protective measures - we have asked for facial distortion of the image - I've asked that the witness be brought in and then these things can go back up, I suppose. And can I be assured that the AV booth is aware? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness will take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Crosland, I understand, sir, that you are a retired colonel with the British army with some 35 years experience; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you were at one point appointed the defence attache to Belgrade from the August of 1996 to the 23rd of March, 1999. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, your role as defence attache, were you in fact accredited to the VJ in that capacity? In other words, were you the accredited attache to liaise with the VJ of the Yugoslav army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I was accredited to General Perisic who was then the chief of defence staff, on behalf of my own chief of defence staff, and accredited solely to the Vojska Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Did you have a lot of dealings with the Ministry of the Interior or MUP?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, we did not except for when I was travelling in Kosovo. Obviously, I then came into contact with the MUP on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And, sir, you left on or about the 23rd of March. Did you then again return, after a hiatus, on the 12th of June, 1999, as a liaison officer for KFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I was then tasked to oversee the withdrawal of the Vojska Yugoslavia and to liaise with them, the VJ and the MUP, and also the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you held that position until mid-July, 1999, I understand?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, is it true that you provided witness statements with respect to your experiences in Kosovo? You provided statements to the investigators of the ICTY on the 25th and 26th of May, 1999, and then again over the 5th through the 7th of December, 2000. Did you provide statements?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, yes, I have the copies with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you have had an opportunity to review the contents of those statements?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I have, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In the course of a recent review, did you note any typographical errors made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Just one, which is the date of 1988 was changed to 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that would be on page 8, I understand, sir, of the statement of May 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In particular -- sorry. It helps if I get the right statement in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Page 8, in the second last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Those paragraphs have been assigned numbers. I believe it's paragraph 40 of -- the second to last paragraph on page 8; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's now paragraph 40, numbered 40. All right. Now, sir, did you also yesterday, on the 9th of July, appear before a presiding officer of this Tribunal and indicate that the contents of these statements were true to the best of your knowledge, information, and belief and make a solemn declaration to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would tender the statements in compliance with Rule 92 bis, with one caveat. I would ask that the date and place of birth marked on the cover sheets be redacted for -- in other words, the copy that the Court can have certainly, I don't have any difficulty with that information being there, but could we have a redacted copy to go into the public record, for security reasons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry, I always do that. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 253.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, while that is being distributed, perhaps I can give the Court a very brief overview of what is contained in these statements and then turn to those portions that I would propose to deal with live. Your Honours, in these statements you will find that Colonel Crosland sets out the various tours that he conducted of Kosovo in his role as Defence attache and the discussions he had with various senior VJ personnel. You will also note that he submitted regular reports in sort of a telegram form to the Ministry of Defence in London and that part of his duties were to assess the build-up of forces. He monitored equipment, vehicles, members of the various PJP and MUP forces in order to provide data to the British ambassador. You will also note that he describes in these statements with some particularity, especially in his background as a military officer, the kinds of uniforms and equipment used by various Serb forces. He outlines for you the identities and positions of various VJ staff members, the various generals, et cetera. He also outlines the incident referred to as the Ahmeti and Jashari massacres in March of -- February and March of 1998. He describes for you his observations of the roles of the PJP, the SAJ, and the JSO, all of which have been referred to in evidence before you. I will lead further evidence about evidence of joint VJ and MUP operations, his understanding or observations of what appeared to be the Pavkovic-Sainovic-Milosevic chain of command; he will deal with the issue of the JSO and someone referred to as Frenki Simatovic, the commander of the JSO in and around Pec. The statement also reviews meetings that he had with General Dimitrijevic and discussions about the KLA, his observations of KLA activity. Then we will be dealing live with what he noted to be a change, a perceived change in the role of the VJ. He will describe for you accompanying Lord Ashdown, who has given evidence here before, on tours of Kosovo, and the evidence of Serb attacks during his 11 visits in Kosovo. He will describe for you a meeting with General Dimitrijevic, and you will see in the statement about his observations towards the end of 1998 the KLA were becoming more organised, the fact that General Perisic was replaced by Colonel General Ojdanic, and also refers in his statement to various other personalities and their roles. I will deal live with his observation of a build-up of forces pre-Christmas 1998, and I will also be dealing with his observations on the 15th of January of the Racak incident. You will be hearing about his observations of burning and looting by VJ and MUP forces in January in various areas and the type of equipment used by a VJ battalion. He will talk about in March 1999 further VJ force build-up. In his statement, you will see the fact that he witnessed on two occasions significant VJ reinforcements being sent to Kosovo and describes their armoured vehicles and the various brigades. Very briefly, Your Honours, he then provides opinions about - as a military man - the capabilities of the combined VJ and MUP forces of being able to displace the bulk of the population. He will deal with the Istok prison visit that he made in June of 1999; and finally, I intend to show him some seven telegram SitReps, which are the situational reports that he prepared which is almost like a contemporaneous note of what he had seen. These are the copies of documents that he provided to the Ministry of Defence. Sort of source documents for some of the opinions that we will be seeking from him. That being the case, then, Your Honours, that is my very brief summary of what is contained in both the statements that you will have, and I propose now to turn to paragraph 6 of my summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I've been reading rather quickly. We speak the same language, but we have to wait for translation. Let's both try to remember to observe a pause, if we can, between question and answer. Now, Colonel Crosland, what capacity were you working -- in what capacity were you working on the 24th of March, 1998, in the Decani area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was working in my capacity as the United Kingdom's defence attache, accompanied by other attaches, and we were touring in the province of Kosovo to ascertain just how serious the situation was becoming of an increasing build-up of Vojska Yugoslavia against what was the Kosovo Liberation Army intrusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And if it assists Your Honours, since I'm dealing with Decani, the Kosovo atlas, page 4, I believe, shows Decani. Right at the bottom of page 4, you will see Decani is right at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, do you have also a map available, Colonel Crosland? Perhaps you can use the ELMO to show from time to time, as and when required, perhaps all on one page, the areas that you were when you made certain observations, during the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I will see if that comes up on the screen. Can the audiovisual please put that on for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it's particularly clear. It's certainly not clear from this end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll just continue to use the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In any event, sir, when you were there, did you note anything regarding the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It was on that visit that we first came across a considerable Vojska Yugoslavia presence in and around Decani which included a large artillery position that we managed to visit which was providing the fire support basically for the western area of Kosovo, from Decani down towards Djakovica and north towards the town of Pec. This artillery position was guarded by elements of the JSO and also other Vojska Yugoslavia units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I understand, sir, that your statement is clear, but for the benefit of those who do not have a copy of your statement, the JSO was what? Was that part of a VJ or a MUP organisation or what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The JSO is part of a MUP special police force, used for -- for both counter-terrorist and for strike action. I'd also say that in all the major towns within Kosovo during that time, there were joint or there were starting to become joint Vojska Yugoslavia and MUP bases. And on many occasions one noticed that Vojska Yugoslavia equipment had been painted into blue colour, which indicated MUP, but it was quite clearly underneath green VJ paint.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you say "Vojska Yugoslavia," that's the official name for what I've been referring to as the Yugoslav army, the VJ?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And from that you're saying that they were repainting army vehicles into police colours? Is that --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I get you. All right. And did you in fact see evidence of that throughout Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I saw throughout Kosovo and throughout the early part of 1998 and the summer and the late autumn numerous vehicles that had been repainted Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. from the Vojska Yugoslavia green to the MUP blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Referring to the MUP for a moment, sir, did you formulate an opinion or -- I'll leave it at that -- of the MUP forces that were capable of being deployed at about that time, in terms of numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The estimate was roughly between 8 to 10.000 were capable of being deployed, and that figure went up and down, depending on the role of the MUP units in Kosovo at the time. That was in addition to the approximate 15.000 of the Vojska Yugoslavia which were stationed there in their normal barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, those were observations, sir, that you saw March and April. Did that develop in July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it did, because up until that period, the KLA had technically taken control of three of the major routes across the province of Kosovo, and it was in about July/August time that the Vojska Yugoslavia and the MUP seemed to combine together to start a clearance operation across the whole of the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, this is something that you saw happening, and did you subsequently have a conversation with General Dimitrijevic concerning your observations on a subsequent occasion? Did you refer to the events that you witnessed in July and August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. Under the constitution of the FRY of Yugoslavia, the Vojska Yugoslavia, who was allowed to maintain control over the borders to initially, I think, 500 metres, that was then further enlarged to two kilometres and eventually out to 20 kilometres. This was partly to do with the deterioration of the current situation. But it was in mid-July when Colonel General Ojdanic then informed the defence attache association in Belgrade, of which I was then the president, that the Vojska Yugoslavia would now defend the lines of communications throughout the province of Kosovo, indicating a much more heavy involvement of the Vojska Yugoslavia in support of the MUP operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On yet a later occasion, did the issue of what they actually did in the summer of 1998 become the subject of discussion with General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I took video film and photographic evidence which indicated artillery of various calibres, main battle tanks, and armoured personnel carriers of the Vojska Yugoslavia in direct support of MUP operations. In other words, they were providing the heavy indirect and direct fire support to MUP ground operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And was that form of assistance within the allowable limits at that stage of the proceedings, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Under the Yugoslavia constitution, no. This was a clear break with what had been the current areas of operation and in part was a knowledge of the deterioration of the situation on the ground within Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you confront General Dimitrijevic with that? And if so, what was his reply?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I informed General Dimitrijevic that we had got evidence, and I think I produced it to himself. I confronted Colonel General Ojdanic at that meeting because he, in front of the defence association, said that the Vojska Yugoslavia was not involved in ground operations, and this was clearly untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there an explanation given for what they did?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As a professional military man, one could see the reason why it was happening. It was the ferocity of these assaults of artillery, main battle tank, and heavy machine-guns from armoured vehicles that was way outside a reasonable level of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Were there any discussions with General Dimitrijevic concerning the relationship of the 3rd Army command and Sainovic and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, there were on two occasions. And on the 3rd of October, we had a meeting with General Dimitrijevic, and on the 5th, at his invitation, with my ambassador where General Dimitrijevic said he was extremely worried about the situation within Kosovo and that General Pavkovic, the commander of the 3rd Army, now currently the chief of defence staff, was working outside the loop of command which went back past General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic to Mr. Milosevic and Sainovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And was there anything unusual about that to your understanding of the normal chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This was totally outside the normal chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was there any further explanation given as to how that would actually work on a step-by-step basis? In other words, who would do what to whom or how did that relationship work? Were you told?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We weren't specifically told, no, but it was fairly obvious to work out that General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic within the Vojska Yugoslavia were not fully informed as to what was going on on the ground in Kosovo and therefore were being excluded from the operational chain of command which went direct from General Pavkovic back to Mr. Milosevic and Sainovic who was his day-to-day operational man.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've referred to the JSO. Do you happen to know who was the commander in charge of the JSO in and around Pec?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. He was a man called Frenki Simatovic, who I met, I think, on one occasion in Pec itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And do you know where the JSO were based?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They had several bases. One was close to the -- an old hotel by Decani monastery, which is in the western side of Kosovo. They had another base in the Istok prison, which is east of Pec, on the road towards Ribnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I could just stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, page 4, at the intersection of 40 and 14.5, describes this area now in the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: And also they had a base at Srbica in the Drenica, between Kumanjia [phoen] and Gornja Trnava [phoen], in the ammunition factory there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When we talk about Istok, is there a prison there by special name?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. There is a very big prison which I refer to as Istok but is sometimes called Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So when you talk about Istok, that's synonymous with Dubrava prison area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. All right. And did you at some point meet with a person who described himself as the commander of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did. On one occasion at least, and that was just before a combat group, which is a combined group. We met on the Pec-Pristina road at a place called Lapusnik, which is about 25 kilometres west from Pristina.
