And within this combat group, there was Vojska Yugoslavia main battle tanks, there was the JSO, there was the SAJ and PJP who were lined up in two bases, one at Lapusnik and one at Kijevo, prior to assaulting Malisevo, which was then the head of or the base for the KLA, Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You may have given a date. If so, it's escaped me. Did you give a date, approximately, when you met this commander of the JSO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It's on the 28th of July, 1998, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did he refer to himself by any name or nickname or name that you happen to recall?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I recall -- I think I recall right, sir, it was Legija, and that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I might, I propose now to move to the summary, paragraphs 11, 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, you have earlier in your statement mentioned the capacities of certain high officials, including officials in the VJ, and I believe you mentioned General Perisic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what was his role when you knew him in the early stages?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I was accredited as the Defence attache to General Perisic who had been the chief of defence staff for about three or four years, and he was defence -- chief of defence staff until replaced by General Ojdanic in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So at some point in October of 1998, General Perisic was relieved of that command function and replaced by General Ojdanic, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And prior to October of 1998, sir, what did you understand the VJ's tasks or duties, largely, were intended to be?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I explained earlier, under the FRY constitution, they had sole task to defend the borders of Yugoslavia. That was out to some 500 metres. That was then extended towards two kilometres and then, finally, out to 20 kilometres. And then in July 1998, Colonel General Ojdanic, who was the Chief of Staff of the Vojska Yugoslavia army then informed the defence attache association that they would now not only defend the borders but also the training areas which they exercised in within Kosovo, some of which were of tactical importance but also the lines of communication across the province of Kosovo. As I indicated, there were four major routes which allowed supplies coming mainly from Serbia to be brought across to the Vojska Yugoslav units and MUP units operating in the western province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. I was asking originally about Perisic. You also referred to a General Pavkovic. Can you tell us what if anything you noted in the summer of 1998 concerning VJ operations involving General Pavkovic, and what was his role in relation to Perisic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It was quite clear from meetings with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic that General Pavkovic was -- had sought -- had seen an opportunity to carry out the wishes, presumably of Mr. Milosevic, and to exert far more operational control direct from Pristina and Nis, his headquarters, in the operations within the Kosovo area. And I believe he saw this as a chance to show that he was willing to carry out the orders of the Yugoslav government outside the normal chain of command which should have gone through the chief of defence staff and General Dimitrijevic, who was the chief of counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you've already alluded to the fact that you've had conversations with these individuals a few moments ago, and I asked you in a different paragraph, but am I right that you in fact discussed these observations about incidents in the summer of 1998 with General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. We had very long conversations, because as a professional soldier, one has been in several situations not dissimilar to what was going on in Kosovo and, therefore, was attempting to give advice as a professional soldier. And it was quite obvious from General Perisic and General Dimitrijevic's demeanour that they were unhappy with the way that operations were now being organised and that the normal chain of command was being relatively ignored in pursuit of a much more aggressive policy which involved the Vojska Yugoslavia, as I've said, in direct support of MUP operations across the province of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, just so I understand the functions and what was happening, I believe you may have expressed this, but I'm going to ask you to clarify for me, if you would, please. What the VJ was doing in the summer of 1998 as you described, was that purely a border thing or was this now being involved in internal security operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Initially within the -- within the early part of 1998, the Vojska Yugoslavia was deployed on the border and particularly on the Albanian and southern and western borders. And then as the operations became more involved, they had to move back to take -- to support the MUP who were incapable, in some respects, of carrying out these particular operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So when they supported the MUP, was that part of a different function? Was that internal security?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, that was bordering on internal security. And this was definitely changed and made formally aware to the defence attaches in July 28th when Colonel General Ojdanic made that statement in front of the attache corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you have a conversation with Perisic and Dimitrijevic concerning whether or not they agreed or disagreed with that type of deployment of the army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: They both were unhappy and disagreed with the heavier involvement, the Vojska Yugoslavia, and said to -- said that to me on at least two occasions, but, rather, said that they were, as I've said already, now more or less outside the regular chain of command and therefore unable to influence, apparently, the situation and the operational tasking that was going direct from Belgrade down to Pristina and Nis, the headquarters of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 3rd Army outside of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've already made reference to the 27th of August, I believe, when General Ojdanic met with the accredited defence attaches and outlined the new policy. Do you -- would this have been before or after you presented the video? I believe you made reference earlier that you had a video. Did you present that video at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I believe I had shown it to General Dimitrijevic who had spoken to General Perisic, and I also produced it for the foreign liaison service after General Ojdanic's speech to the accredited defence attache association.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And what did this video show? What was it of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It showed Vojska Yugoslavia units, heavy artillery, and main battle tanks working within the central region of Kosovo in and around, I believe, Suva Reka, Blace, and Dulje areas, which were then under fairly constant bombardment as a part of the "clearance," in inverted commas, operations that were ongoing throughout July, August, and September of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, perhaps you can assist us. Your familiarity of the geography of Kosovo; the locations of Junik, Prilep, Rznic, and Glodjane, where are those villages located? Generally in what area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These are all in between the western town of Djakovica and Decani, about 10 kilometres south of Decani, and in towards what was called the Jablanica area. The small villages of Rznic and Prilep were just on the main road and just off the main road. We were taken there in I think it was August because there had been a massacre at a place called Glodjane. Whilst we were taken under escort, having been met in Djakovica by the MUP, we actually went past troops still on operations, which included elements from the Vojska Yugoslavia, the SAJ, the JSO, and the PJP, who, as we drove past, were still torching, burning, and firing into various houses as we were driven through, this armoured convoy, and we eventually arrived at the small village of Glodjane. The MUP who brought us there indicated in the deep water channel had been a massacre, and I myself saw six to eight bodies that had been shot, and there were bullet marks on the concrete of the water channel. Who these people were was impossible to tell because we were not allowed to go close to the bodies concerned, but the MUP commander from Djakovica informed me that these were Serb -- Kosovo Serbs who had been killed by the local KLA. But as I said, we could not confirm that. But there were definitely six to eight bodies there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, did that incident that you've just told us about that you witnessed, this continual firing, was that raised at all on the 28th of August with Ojdanic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And he, Colonel General Ojdanic, really didn't seem to want to know what was going on in truth. It was witnessed by myself and other defence attaches that, despite what was being portrayed from Belgrade, the truth was very far from that within the province of Kosovo and that many of the operations were extremely heavy-handed. I myself saw over -- between 2 and 300 villages burnt throughout 1998, 1999. Crops were just wantonly burnt. Businesses of all sorts were routed and looted. Petrol stations, any shops. And within towns like Decani, Pec, and Djakovica, the Albanian areas were completely burnt out. And this included damage to mosques, which I, amongst other people, informed the Vojska Yugoslavia was not the clever way of doing operations. So there was significant civilian damage done purely to drive out civilians from both their homes, their farms, and also from the towns that I indicated of Pec, Decani, and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry to come back to this topic, but those four villages that you mentioned by name - Junik, Prilep, Rznic, and Glodjane - you described to us what you saw. Was the incident of what you witnessed there the subject of discussion with Ojdanic, and if so, did he say anything to you, having been confronted with that, about how that might be viewed in terms of security or humanitarian concerns?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not really, sir. I mean, I think he found it difficult to understand. I mean, for instance, Your Honours, the very small hamlet of Prilep on the Decani-Djakovica road was probably 40 to 50 centimetres high; all the houses been bulldozed flat. That is the level of destruction we're talking about, and that was throughout. In certain areas throughout Kosovo, major destruction had taken place, and people - certainly Colonel General Ojdanic - did not seem to want to hear this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Moving to paragraph 12, if I may, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, during the course of your duties, I understand that Lord Ashdown was also a visitor to Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. He -- I think if I remember rightly, he carried out two visits, and I accompanied him with our ambassador on both these visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When would that have been, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: One was in the latter part of September, I believe the 26th, 27th, but they were about four or five days, so it spread over a good period within Kosovo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just without getting into a lot of detail of the tour, what areas did you visit with Lord Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We carried out, Your Honours, a comprehensive tour throughout all of Kosovo, but in this particular time we concentrated on the area around Suva Reka, Dulje, Blace, and we were accompanied by the BBC who filmed footage of ongoing operations that were quite clearly Vojska Yugoslavia supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you have access to the footage taken by the BBC that was travelling?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I have seen that, and it was transmitted, I believe, on that evening news.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you also take any video or photographic evidence of what you had seen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And later on, did you have a meeting with General Ojdanic in the presence of Lord Ashdown?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I believe we did, sir, yes. And again, Lord Ashdown also went to see Mr. Milosevic directly after his visit to Kosovo, on one occasion at least, and I believe also made those comments to Mr. Milosevic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Paragraph 13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Between July and October, then - this is sort of summary - how many visits did you make to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I made approximately 11 visits, Your Honours, and these were sometimes of three, four, five, and six days duration. So I spent a lot of the late summer and early autumn in Kosovo. Also on behest of Mr. Holbrooke when the initiative there was being attempted to be signed in late October, November. And I actually supervised the withdrawal, as on the plan of Mr. Holbrooke, of the Vojska Yugoslavia units back to their barracks in Pristina, in Prizren, and in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And on those visits, on each of those visits, did you see evidence of incidents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They were continuous -- there were continually burnings and lootings from villages, and some villages had been looted and burnt at least on three occasions, with the civilian population leaving and then returning once they thought it was relatively safe to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that I'm clear about that, when you say three times, you mean they'd burn, they'd leave, they'd come back, it would be burned again, they'd leave, come back, burned again? Is that what you mean by three times?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's exactly correct, sir, yes. Because the civilian population would move out to the woods. Bearing in mind it was a very warm summer, but then coming in towards the autumn, the temperature drops quickly. The only shelter they had was either in the woods or back in their dilapidated buildings, which then were starting to get some UNHCR help in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know what time you want to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to try and do this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we started at 10.35, so you've got another quarter of an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Wonderful. I'm just hoping to try to get through this before the break, but I had no idea as to when that break will be. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Paragraph 14. Sir, I'll move on a little more quickly. You have already referred to a 3rd of October, 1998, meeting with General Dimitrijevic, and now as part of that discussion, part of which you've already related, did you discuss with General Dimitrijevic some of the air defence assets that you had personally observed in the -- and their use against civilians?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Throughout 1998, many of the -- or nearly all of the air defence assets - and these are armoured vehicles, wheeled vehicles and semi-tracked vehicles, what they all BOV 3s and Pragas - were used in the direct fire role against villages, and I personally saw that happen on numerous occasions. And this was a tactic of a standoff, direct attack onto a village in order to destroy the infrastructure of that village and drive any of the population who might have been there out of their own personal houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: From your observations, these villages, did they appear to be apparent military targets?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. These were normal civilian villages. Inevitably in some of these villages there would be supporters of the Kosovo Liberation Army because, as you're well aware, the population within Kosovo is probably about a million plus Albanians, or it was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And to your understanding of the Geneva Convention, was that type of behaviour permissible?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not at all. These are 20, 30, and 40-millimetre cannon, which are very destructive and are used, under the Geneva Convention, for use against aircraft and/or other armoured vehicles but certainly not against personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, is there a group or body known as the HMA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The HMA is Her Majesty's Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. So when you met with Dimitrijevic, you met in the presence of the then ambassador for Britain, is that Ambassador Donnelly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, yes. And it was on his -- on my return from Kosovo and on my ambassador's wishes to speak with the most senior person we could do in order to attempt to rationalise a situation that was rapidly becoming out of hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in the company of Her Majesty's Ambassador -- I take it he was present for this October 3rd meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And so was there any discussions concerning the responsibility for Kosovo at that point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I believe my ambassador made it perfectly clear that he was holding Mr. Milosevic and the Vojska Yugoslavia and MUP responsible for what was going on in Kosovo and indicated that future action may be taken against those who were responsible for quite clearly crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, was there also a report where you got a message about the MUP PJP detachments operating in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It was during this time under Mr. Holbrooke's initiative various MUP units were redeployed out of Kosovo, and I personally witnessed them moving out. However, not very long afterwards, other MUP/PJP units were brought back in to replace those who had been on duty for three or four months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So there appeared to be an initial compliance and then things changed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The Vojska Yugoslavia, as I've said earlier, I personally saw the three battle groups return to their barracks and signal this back to the relevant authorities. We also, as I've said, saw the withdrawal of certain elements of the MUP/PJP, and then we saw other elements coming back in over a period of days, replacing those who had been sent back out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It was a matter of days before other units replaced them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As far as I recall, Your Honours, within a week to two-week period, yes, so the status quo was regained in terms of numbers of Serbian security forces within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very quickly skipping down to paragraph 18, just before Christmas, around the 19th, the 21st of December, 1998, did you witness anything in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relation to the 211 Brigade from Nis?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This brigade from Nis, which we could very easily identify by various signs it had on it, was deployed to the west on the high ground just outside of Podujevo, along the main supply route which went back to Krsumlija Banja, which is an advances headquarters for 3rd Army from Nis, and therefore, they were protecting their main supply route from the KLA who mounted various attacks within that area. But this was a battalion-plus sizing deployment and also down onto an airfield called Donje Pudenje [phoen] where they had another battalion-minus. So there was, in effect, just under a brigade of armour, including main battle tanks, armoured personnel carriers, and artillery within and around the Podujevo environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And again I'm sorry, being a non-military person, you may have to state the obvious for my benefit. When you saw tanks, was that MUP or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. The Vojska Yugoslavia maintained control of all main battle tanks and in particular some units were equipped with the later T-84, which indicated that these were units mainly external from Kosovo. They were from either Nis or even from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So this 211 Brigade from Nis, that was definitely an army brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And a brigade is approximately how many men or how many --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: In rough terms, between 3 and 4.000, depending on how much strength it had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. This is a large group of people.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It is a very large and a very powerful organisation, and they did considerable damage to the villages just west of Podujevo; Bradas, Dobratin, Gornja Lapastica and Donje Lapastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you see any MUP at the same time as you saw this 211 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the headquarters there in Podujevo and also saw, within the perimeter areas, both a combined MUP and VJ presence, and it was quite clear they were working together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One further question on that topic then, sir. As a military man seeing these many people and MUP and police obviously working together, did you form any opinion or speculation as to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It -- Your Honours, it indicated how serious the Vojska Yugoslavia was taking the situation, which was deteriorating with an influx of Kosovo Liberation Army people and equipment. And it was also obviously protecting their major route back into southern Serbia up towards Prokuplje and on to Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were you concerned at all about what you witnessed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Very concerned, Your Honours, in that every time there was an operation, there was a completely unreasonable use of force put in against the villages and towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel Crosland, I want to take you now, if you would, please, to the 15th of January, 1999, referred to as Racak. Can you tell the Court in some detail, if you would, in this particular area, I'm going to take -- where were you, what time were you there, what did you see? I'm just going to let you explain for the Court how you happened to be there, where you were, and what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, the small village of Racak is just west of a place called Stimlje, which is on the -- one of the southern routes across to Suva Reka and on to Prizren. Stimlje was a joint Vojska Yugoslavia and MUP outpost, because just beyond Racak was a small village of Crnoljevo which was really where the Kosovo Liberation Army had a quasi-control over this mountainous road that went up towards Dulje where the Vojska Yugoslavia had a combat group in a fairly isolated position up on the heights that overlooked the village of Suva Reka. If I recall correctly, there was an attack on a MUP - maybe also VJ - patrol just west of the village of Racak, which resulted, I think, if I remember rightly, in three MUP being killed. And it was then quite clear that a major operation would be mounted using Colonel Delic's 243 Brigade from Urosevac, the Vojska Yugoslavia formation, and all the combined elements of the PJP/MUP to take out what was disclosed as a Kosovo Liberation Army headquarters, in their terminology. I would just say a base, but that can be debated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there just to clarify something. This incident that you referred to about two or three individuals being killed, was that on the 15th or was that some days before the 15th or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think if I recall rightly, sir, it was a couple of days prior to the major operation against Racak which was on the overnight 14th/15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. So -- thank you. It was sometime prior to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: -- to the Racak incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. It probably was the catalyst for this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see. Sorry to have interrupted.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Not at all, sir. I arrived, I think, mid-afternoon, about 2.00, in the area, and there was a - and had been - a continuous bombardment of M-80s, which are armoured personnel vehicles, about nine of them on the high ground overlooking Racak, and they were supported by D-30s, which are howitzers, manned by Vojska Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, how did you come to know that there would be an operation in Racak at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, the Kosovo KVM, Kosovo Verification Mission was also in the area and attempting to monitor the ongoing operations. And by the amount of troops, both the MUP in all its elements and the Vojska Yugoslavia concentrating in that area, it was very clear that an operation was about to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is that why you attended Racak?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. In -- you tend to get, having been in the area for as long as I've been, a feel for what is going on. And this was an extremely dangerous and difficult area for the Yugoslav authorities to have any control over because they needed to, as I've indicated, as one of their main supply routes westwards to Suva Reka and then on to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I cut across His Honour's question. I might use this opportunity now to ask you again. You referred to, I think it was M-80s, a continuous bombardment of M-80s, it says in the transcript. Oh, you said they were armoured personnel vehicles. Are they like tanks or --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. These are smaller armoured vehicles which have heavy machine-guns and can lay down a considerable amount of firepower. And as I said, there were about nine of these vehicles, firing more or less continuously into and around the area of Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And could you determine where this equipment was from or whether it was JNA or MUP or -- were there tanks there as well or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: There were elements of the Vojska Yugoslavia from -- we recognised from 243 brigade which is the Mechanised Brigade out of Urosevac. It was that brigade's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see any tanks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we saw some T55s.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. Again I interrupted. The size of this operation, sir, that you witnessed, what level of, shall we say, in the normal chain of command, what level of knowledge or planning or operational cooperation do you think there would have to have been for something like to take place?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, there must have been a close cooperation between the 52 Corps was the VJ corps based in Pristina, under command of General Lazarevic, who I knew and had seen on many occasions and given sustenance to Vojska Yugoslavia soldiers who had been wounded and, in fact, one killed. I went to see the bodies and gave medical aid to their sick soldiers who had been wounded. And that's documented in other areas. But it was quite clear that there had been a coordinated move between the Vojska Yugoslavia and the MUP to clear out this nest of the KLA and, I suppose, to teach the KLA a lesson. But it seemed to me a very blunt way of doing it, directly under the noses of then Ambassador Walker's Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you see members of the Kosovo Verification Mission there while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. I believe it was Ambassador Walker, but I can't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps you would -- were you there when the actual conflict occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I arrived just after the major conflict had arrived. But there was considerable activity ongoing that afternoon and throughout that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I believe Their Honours would like to know what you actually witnessed. Who was doing what to whom, when, and where?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It was quite clear for me the way the M-80s, the armoured personnel vehicles were on the ridgeline above Stimlje that overlooked the village of Racak, that they were providing what we would call intensive covering fire into the area of Racak itself. I then believe there was what we would call a sweep operation which went through Racak. And if I remember correctly, there were seven or eight members of the Kosovo Liberation Army brought out who had been killed. The other people who had been killed, many of them had extremely close burn marks, indicating they had been shot from very close range. Obviously I was not present when they were shot, but one has seen enough, sadly, enough bodies in one life to realize that these people had been shot from very close range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, did you hear or see the exchange of gunfire at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You could have heard it nearly back in Pristina. This was a very, very serious engagement, and a complete, in my opinion, a complete flouting of the authority of the Kosovo Verification Mission, because they would -- I believe Ambassador Walker arrived with the world's press, who got not as close as we got but were very clearly able to see the nine armoured vehicles firing directly at Racak and the other units that were spread around the Stimlje area who were in support of this operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you -- does it mean that you saw the -- some fight back from the KLAs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was impossible to see that, Your Honour, because they are down the other side of the hill, totally overlooked by the Serbian security force position. It's a wooded position which would obviously allow some people to have slipped away southwards. But on the Serbian side, it was very much a bare valley leading from their position down towards Racak itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just to clarify, if I may. Picking up from where His Honour's question left off, when you responded to His Honour's question about an exchange of gunfire and you answered in the way you did, were you focusing on the word "exchange" or were you focusing on the --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. Sorry. It was very difficult to know whether there was any fire coming back. The weight of fire going down was -- was extremely heavy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your duties at Racak, visit the area known as the gully after the fact?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I did not go down into that area because access was restricted. I think Ambassador Walker went down, and one or two people from KVM.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You did not personally?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I did not personally go down there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you able to give us a time frame as to when you witnessed this heavy artillery being shot into Racak? Approximately when are we talking?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, sir, it was from mid-morning of the 14th or the 15th. I think it was mid-morning of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Until?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Until late afternoon on the 15th, I would suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And your observation point? Like, where, approximately, would you have been in order to witness this?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: We managed to get reasonably close to Stimlje by various routes that we'd worked out from before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: And there's absolutely no -- the definition of who was involved was absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Were there KVM observers in approximately the same opportunity to witness the incident; i.e., was their vantage point known to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: There was a vantage point known to me. The KVM, as far as I recall, were not allowed in. I think Ambassador Walker was then allowed in with various people, after the operation, to see what had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would the KVM, to your knowledge, have been in a position to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. observe the same incident you did and would have had an opportunity to make known their observations to people within their chain of command?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I would have thought so, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, if you're going to move from Racak --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- it may be a convenient moment to break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's -- yes. I'm about to go to paragraph 20, 23, 25, and 27. That's all I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Nonetheless, given the time constraints --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- it may not be possible to finish the colonel's evidence today. Colonel, we'll do the best to finish your evidence today, but I'm afraid I can't promise that we'll be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I should warn you formally not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include members of the Prosecution team. However, if arrangements have to be made for you to come back sometime to complete your evidence between now and the summer or the early autumn, perhaps you could have a word with Mr. Ryneveld about that, just that particular point, to try and find a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, perhaps you could report on those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I might say I don't believe it will be necessary for me to speak to the witness in between. Out of an abundance of caution, we have canvassed that, what I hoped was a remote possibility, and I do believe that the witness might be able to make himself available first thing Monday morning if he can get out of here mid-morning sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Right. That sounds satisfactory. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, returning very rapidly to Marjan Krasniqi referred to by the accused this morning, his statements having been reviewed, the position is that his statements are subject to the full 92 bis procedure carried out in the region earlier this year on the 13th of March at a time when we were intending to make him part of our case. As the Chamber knows, we've radically reduced the number of witnesses since then, but he remains a potentially useful witness. And since the accused wants his statements in, I give notice now under 92 bis that I apply for his statements, in accordance with the package of documents provided to the accused and the Court, should be adduced subject to the full provisions of 92 bis. That is to say they can simply be read into evidence. It would be surprising if the accused were to challenge that, as he's asked for the statements to go into evidence. The normal timing under 92 bis is 14 days -- 7 days and 14 days, I think, but I'd ask for an appropriate abbreviation so that the accused can make his position clear as to whether this witness is required for cross-examination or not. One would assume not in light of his own application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Outstanding, then, is the position of Mr. Coo. The Court raised a very practical solution to the problem yesterday simply as a possibility, giving his evidence in chief before de la Billiere were to be called. The only potential problem is that is the normal rule that a witness would not be communicating about his evidence with the Office of the Prosecutor once he's started to give evidence. That hardly applies with the same force if it's only examination-in-chief of an expert, and subject to a resolution of that difficulty, if the Court is minded to pursue that possibility, we would be only too happy to go along with it. But there's one technical issue that we'd like to be resolved in order to help the Court: His exhibits are currently not in a tabbed or divided format. There's a problem about putting tabs on documents or putting numbers on documents that as soon as you change a document at all, you have to have it resubmitted for the whole processing -- process of having numbers put on it and so on and so forth. I'm sure that for future 92 bis exhibits we can find a solution to this that won't waste people's time and have documents being numbered twice. As to Mr. Coo's exhibits, we are only too happy to do anything that would assist the management of the exhibits. In particular if it would be thought appropriate for those documents to be placed into tabbed binders, we could do that for their more easy handling. But that's that. But it would help us to know if we can call him on that basis, and we'll get on and make appropriate preparations, discussing the mechanics of handling the exhibits with your legal officer as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is in the evidence of Mr. Coo, in any event, a challenge to admissibility of parts. If you're going to oppose what the amici have suggested, then we'll need to have a hearing on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think it will be particularly long, but we're going to submit a written document, I hope today or tomorrow, to narrow the issues. And then finally, we've served the statement of Isuf Jemini, the cousin of the man who overheard the observations from his building. We've been granted leave to call him. Can I give notice that we will seek to call him at any convenient time in the next two weeks? He's the sort of witness who may serve as a useful witness to take a little time if we otherwise fall short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has his statement been disclosed yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. It was disclosed in the application to call him, and the application was granted, so it's been disclosed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you. I believe I was about to turn to paragraph 20 of the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, I'm going to summarise just a little bit here. I understand, sir, that during your various tours you've already testified about having seen destruction, burning, and looting of some of the villages. Did that also occur in 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it did, Your Honours, in the area around Podujevo where the Vojska Yugoslavia had deployed 211 Brigade from Nis and at least 3 villages, four villages - Gornja Lapastica, Donja Lapastica, Bradas, and Dobratin - were heavily destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For Your Honours, that's -- those villages can be seen on page 3 of the Kosovo atlas.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I've been cautioned to pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, did you note a VJ battalion involved in what you witnessed in those villages you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The direct and indirect fire was coming from equipment which was manned by Vojska Yugoslavia and also by MUP elements, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. PJP probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And very briefly, can you describe the method of operation that you witnessed? In other words, who did what, in what order, to whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It appeared that on most operations, warning shots would be fired into the area of the villages that were about to be assaulted, presumably to try and warn the civilian population that worse was to come, and then there would be a very destructive phase of bombardment which would then be followed up by a ground operation which, as I addressed previously, would be torching and burning and looting of the houses concerned that were still standing. Also the crops, both in the field adjacent to the houses and in much wider areas throughout the middle of Kosovo, which is a fairly agriculture area and really the breadbasket of Kosovo itself, particularly the area around Kijevo, in the middle, was burning for probably several weeks as various fires were lit throughout the summer and late autumn of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: To your observation, what effect, if any, did the burning of the crops have on the ability of the villagers to return at some later time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think initially this caused considerable distress. Also their livestock was slaughtered in a very wanton way. Towards the end of 1998 when the UNHCR and other aid agencies started to get food and materials back into the area, it was not quite so destructive, but why it was done, I'm afraid I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: One further question on this particular paragraph, sir: You've told us the method that you saw things happen. What forces would be involved in the looting or the ground operation, I believe that you've called it? Would that be the army again or would that be someone else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Most of the -- most of the ground operations that I came across, the direct fire and indirect fire support would be provided by the Vojska Yugoslavia, and the assault troops would come from either the JSO, PJP or the SAJ units who would then move through the area and systematically clear it and carry out most of the destructive work. Obviously the shell-fire and gunfire from the Vojska Yugoslavia and other elements would be very destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In your military experience, would there have to be any coordination between the army and the ground forces in order to avoid friendly-fire casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I'm sure there must have been a coordination centre, presumably in Pristina, where joint operations were planned in order to prevent what we would term blue-on-blue but also prevent artillery and other long-range fire going into areas that other Serbian security forces may be involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you witnessed these operations, did you see what the villagers did during these operations that you've talked about? What did the villagers do?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, most -- most times, as far as I was aware, as I said, there would be warning shots fired in the area of the village in order to drive out the villagers before the major attack took place. And therefore, the attacks, certainly onto areas like Malisevo and other villages around that area, probably the majority of the villagers had left, and therefore troops just swept through and wantonly destroyed, and, if you like, ethnically cleansed, or attempted to ethnically cleanse, these areas and succeeded really in pushing, certainly in the area of Malisevo down towards the Podgorusa valley, in excess of 30 to 40.000 villagers who were camping out for most of the summer and late autumn of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: These villages that you've referred to, sir, in your experience in Kosovo, were you familiar with the ethnic composition of the majority of the inhabitants of those villages?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The majority of these villages were Kosovo Albanian. The major Serb villages were like -- were places like Kijevo, which is a Serb stronghold in the middle of Kosovo. And then most of the other Serbs -- Kosovo Serbs were in amongst the major towns of Pristina, Pec, and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you make any observations in 1998 and early 1999 about the Serb neighbourhoods of those towns or Serb villages? What -- did you note any similar destruction in regard to those areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No. Most of these Serb enclaves became no-go areas to the likes of myself and were guarded by local defence units which were all organised on a sort of territorial basis of villagers who were armed and guarded their own properties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Now, your statement refers to the issues in paragraph 23. In order for time, I'm going to skip that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours may want to note that at page 3, the intersection of 20 and 06 would assist for the location of those areas in paragraph 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I want to move on, if I may, to the Istok or Dubrava Prison visit you made in June of 1999. That premises, as I understood it -- you understood it to have been bombed at one point?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. It was bombed during a campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And did you visit after the conflict was over?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. I visited in early June, and when we arrived in the area with another defence attache, we found a whole mass of documents, which some purported to be execution orders. There were certainly -- these were handed over to the relevant authorities, along with licna kartas, identity cards and other forms of identity that obviously had been stripped off various individuals which were just inside the main wall adjacent to the major control point in front of Istok or Dubrava Prison, as it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, quick question, sir: In the course of your duties, did you learn to read or understand the Serbian language in either Cyrillic or in the normal writing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Before taking up the appointment, I learnt Serbian and both Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And these documents that you saw, you personally looked at some of them, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I did indeed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And could you determine these identity cards and documents, what ethnicity of individuals they referred to or are you able to voice an opinion concerning that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These documents concerned Kosovo Albanian persons and were both identity cards and some were of -- for execution orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the course of your duties, I believe you mentioned earlier that you would prepare reports or summaries in order to notify the people to whom you were responsible. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I produced about roughly 70 -- from 70 tours. These tours stretched from one day to the outside of a week in duration.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And were you present and did you provide information to Her Majesty's Ambassador at that time as well?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I naturally worked very closely with my ambassador who also linked in with the political chain of command in Belgrade as the situation deteriorated throughout 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And some of these reports which may have been under the signature of Her Majesty's Ambassador Donnelly, would you have had an input or be familiar with the contents of many of those documents?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I provided most of the military detail because I was based for a long, long period -- a long period in Kosovo and, therefore, contributed towards the report on the military and geographical side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, then, Your Honours, I propose very briefly to show the witness a series of some seven documents which are outlined in paragraph 27. In order to avoid confusion, I'm going to do them one at a time, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The first document, Colonel Crosland, bares the date of May 11th and 12th. Perhaps Madam Usher could assist us in distributing those. Do you have a copy of that SitRep available to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I have a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You have your own copy of that document? We'll wait until Their Honours get their copy. And we'll just describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we get all of them at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You want the whole bundle?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have the bundle together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies, Your Honours. Do we have a bundle now? No. The case manager's going to have to sort those. Perhaps I can deal with the first one while that's being done. I don't want to -- and that's my fault and I apologise for not having them in bundles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The first document, sir, maybe you can just describe the format of this so that we know what we're talking about. The first document has a number R0118465, and it appears to be confidential. And then it's Britmilrep Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We need to have these first.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought Your Honours had been given the first one. My apologies. I'll wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is -- it really would be helpful to have these together in future, clipped together so it's convenient for everybody. How far are we in a position to go now?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We don't want to waste any time on it. We're now getting a third one. K2490 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There are seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There are seven and I think that the total number of pages would be 15 or 20 pages, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us start with whichever one you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I was going to do them in chronological order, at least in which they were written. The first one is the 11th and 12th of May, and you can see that, and it says: "Subject: Kosovo SitRep as at 11/12 May 1998." Does Your Honour have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll let that have an exhibit number. We'll give them each separate exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 254.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, this particular document, you're familiar with the details of it? You were the source of much of the information, were you, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, yes. I wrote this document and most of the other ones, and it's following a very simple format. It gives you the title at the top, the day and the date concerned, and then a summary of the key points and then detail of various areas that we came across and is designed to brief people as to the situation that we incurred during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And in this first document, you refer to the situation in area Ponosevac, Djakovica -- I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: The area concerned, Your Honours, is Ponosevac, which is on the western fringe between Djakovica and Decani, which was an extremely tense area bordering the Albanian border and therefore a prime area of interest for the Serb security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And in paragraph number 2, did you make some observations there of what the villages south of Ponosevac looked like or what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of these villages from the outskirts of Djakovica up towards Ponosevac and on towards Decani have been severely damaged. Most of the civilian population had left and it was being patrolled by elements from the JSO and the PJP in what I've described as a very heavy-handed fashion; i.e., firing at any livestock that happened to be alive and destroying or adding to the destruction already carried out in the areas of the homesteads of the civilian population who had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. That's been given a number. I turn next, if I may, to the one dated 28 May 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked Prosecutor's Exhibit 255.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: This appears to be a four-page document. And do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Very quickly. Under the summary, the first paragraph on page 1, you refer there to seeing the villages north of Decani. Can you tell us Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about that.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: These villages, Your Honour, are on the major western road from Djakovica through Decani up to Pec and particularly in the area of Gornji Streoc, and Prilep, and Rznic that we've already spoken about. These villages had suffered heavy damage. And again, most of the population was either too frightened to appear or they had actually left the area, moved towards the area of Junik, which is west of this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning to the next page of this exhibit, under the heading numbered 2, Restriction of Movement, did you attempt access at Zrze?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and we were refused permission. Zrze is a small hamlet just north-west of -- sorry, south-west of Djakovica, and it was then a -- I believe a VJ and a MUP control point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In paragraph number 3, did you make some observations about the village of Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This village is in the middle of the Drenica area, just south of it, and was throughout the entire period of 1998 to 1999 a Serb-controlled stronghold backed up by MUP and PJP and remained in Serb hands throughout the period 1998 to 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. The bottom of that page, I believe under numbered 4, burning in villages north of Decani. And then over the top, on the third page, what observations did you make in that report there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Basically, Your Honours, in this area there were very few other vehicles on the road apart from ourselves and most of the villages at Ljubenic and Gornji Streoc had been extremely heavily damaged. Their population had either left or was staying hidden for fear of any further retaliation. And the area was rather like a deserted area apart from the vehicle checkpoints or what we call vehicle checkpoints of the MUP and the PJP that were distributed along this area in an attempt to hold the western boundary on this road itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Paragraph numbered 5.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This is referring to the area south of Klina, which is in the central area of Kosovo and involved the village of Dolovo down towards Rakovica. Again, there was a transit route for the Serbian security forces, and these villages overlooked this route and had therefore been fired at and, as I reported in this report, fairly large fires were burning throughout that day, which was more or less a very common and daily occurrence throughout 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Paragraph 6. Did you see any helicopter attacks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. There were various reports indicating helicopters. We saw one Hind, which is a particularly aggressive helicopter, flying in the area of Pec -- sorry, Kosovska Mitrovica, late in 1998, but otherwise we saw very little helicopter activity primarily because the Vojska Yugoslavia does not have many helicopters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Over the page, sir, rather than spend any time on it, you've already testified having seen vehicles painted in various colours. You made reference about repainting in paragraph 9; is that correct? You've already testified about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, and that was in general evidence throughout all the joint Vojska Yugoslavia MUP compounds or garrison areas as well as out in the countryside, and they were deployed on operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm just been advised that these documents we're now dealing with, the OTP reference numbers were 2490, we've just dealt with 2491, and the balance of the bundle you have go from 2493 do 2496, for ease of reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel Crosland, on the same document, number 10, could you clarify the meaning of "MUP turning the screw too"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That is a typing error. The phrase "turning the screw" is really an English phrase, applying a lot more pressure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there's a typing error there, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just -- what do you mean by that expression, they were applying more pressure? To what? To whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: It appeared that the actions of the Serbian security forces, to use a blanket term, would involve the attempted complete dislocation of village life by burning the crops outside, by destroying any haystacks; i.e., winter food for the animals, by slaughtering any animals that they came across; horses, cows, et cetera, and then the wanton destruction of private citizens' houses and also the looting and destruction of any businesses that were useful or not useful to the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the next document, the next SitRep, the 30th of July, 1998. Exhibit number, Madam Clerk?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 256.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I want to go very quickly, if I may, sir. Page 1, you talk about meeting an assault force of SAJ, PJP and VJ in relation to Malisevo. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This was -- this refers to we had come up south through Malisevo which in July was the KLA's headquarters, or one of their headquarters, and we then met this combat group commanded by the SAJ, but linked to it was elements of the Vojska Yugoslavia with their tanks, other elements of the JSO, PJP, both at Kijevo and Lapusnik. There were two strike forces that were poised to attack down towards Malisevo which, later in that day, they carried out, including one of their vehicles being mined just south of Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On the following page where there are -- where the numbers 3, 4, and 5 are written rather than in numerical number, you make some comments. I believe you already testified about what you saw in your evidence. These are just the backup documents that you made at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Basic -- as I said, we put a summary so that people could read the major summary and get the flavour for it, and then if they wanted the detail, we put in the detail, as you can see, in those particular paragraphs, but it refers to the two strike forces that we encountered at Lapusnik and Kijevo prior to the operation towards Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And on the following page, under the heading Bravo near the top of page 3 of this document, it says "wanton damage, every village." And then you describe again the same methodology that you described earlier in your evidence today?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I -- I personally had driven up from Malisevo just prior to meeting the Serbian security forces on the main road, and all these houses were undamaged, and these crops were unburnt. So this was done directly afterwards when they made the assault. And as it says in Charlie, I then took the troika group of ambassadors down towards this area and they saw for themselves the amount of damage that had been done following this assault onto the Malisevo area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. 7th of August, 1998, SitRep.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Next number, Madam Clerk.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 257.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Again, quickly, sir. This refers to an incident on the 5th and 6th of August, and you wrote the report on the 7th. You talked about Drenica, Junik, and Jablanica areas. And again you talked about the destruction and damage to infrastructure, crops, businesses in the same way that you've witnessed in other areas?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. This was happening all through the middle part of the summer, July, August, and September, when the Serbian security forces were attempting to regain control of the area. And it appeared that their tactics were to -- to try and drive the civilian population out of these areas by destroying their houses and burning and looting any existing businesses or any other areas that might interest them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Then over the next page, under number 2, you refer to "Civpop." I take it that means the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What in particular were you recording there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Throughout this period in July, August, and September, there was a massive internal movement of internally displaced persons, IDPs, who were the civilian population of the various areas attacked, and they were driven from their homes and took refuge in either nearby forests or actually moved further south to get to larger areas, like the Podgorusa valley which is just north of Suva Reka. So there was very much a transient civilian population that was just trying to keep out of the way of the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Next SitRep, dated September 1998. I believe this refers to a situation on the 8th and 9th of September.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I don't know whether Your Honours have that. Thank you. In due course, perhaps we could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 257.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Page -- first -- front page, numbered 2. IDP, is that the internally displaced persons that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. That's an acronym used, internally displaced people. And as I've already said, it was in the area north of Suva Reka which was held by the Serbian security forces, sandwiched between there and Malisevo, which was also held by the Serbian security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How many people did you see in that cluster?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: This -- Your Honours, this varied between, as I put down here, 5 and 15.000 people, and it went up to somewhere in the region of 30 to 40.000 at times. It's -- it was a more or less impossible task to ascertain because people were living under ponchos or under polyethene bags or in hedges or anywhere they could to get out of the sun and the elements and in just huge groups that were really very difficult to count. But the general information was between 5 and 15.000 on this occasion, but it rose higher than that later in the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In points 3 through 6 on the following page, I believe you make some observations about seeing the destruction of the villages. And at point 7, did you make any assessment as to what lay in store for these people in the winter months?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It was of great interest to the Kosovo Verification Mission, KDOM, and also who had to coordinate the civilian aid that was by now starting to come in, and as you see there, there was outlined figures of 171.000. But again, as I said, it's very difficult to estimate completely accurately this situation. And the attempt by the UNHCR and other non-governmental organisations to bring in aid was to try and prevent a catastrophe happening over the coming winter months where the villagers who had had their houses destroyed and their crops burnt would have no food for them to eat or their animals who had been killed didn't need food anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Turning then to the next one of the 3rd of October 1998, this document refers --

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I address the Court to avoid double numbering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Something seems to have gone wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The previous one should have been 258 and the new one should be 259, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I may then turn to the 3rd of October, 1998. Is that now 259 or is that 260? 259? Thank you. Sir, you've given some evidence about meetings that you had with, among others, Dimitrijevic on the 3rd of October, and you've told us -- does this document -- is that more or less a more contemporaneous document with the conversation that you had with Dimitrijevic, or a summary of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honours. It is a detailed summary of the meeting with General Dimitrijevic where he quite clearly wanted to disassociate himself and the Chief of Staff from what was going on under General Pavkovic's arrangements in theatre in Kosovo and also from the direct chain of command that went from Mr. Milosevic to General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: And I think we covered that in quite a lot of detail already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I don't intend to belabour that point. But basically, this is a more contemporaneous memorandum you made immediately after that October 3rd meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it was, sir, with -- Your Honours, with also input from my ambassador who began to realise the situation was getting extremely Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. demanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that Their Honours are clear, I believe you told us that Her Majesty's Ambassador was also present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And finally, sir -- I believe it's finally, yes -- the 6th of November 1998. Now, on page -- I am sorry, I guess I need a number. 261, would it be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecutor's Exhibit 260.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: 260, thank you. Paragraph 2, there was a further request to meet with General Dimitrijevic on the 5th of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time it was a mutual request from both me and General Dimitrijevic to meet to further discuss what was currently a very rapidly deteriorating situation, and the details are in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. And I want to draw your attention to paragraph 5. I asked you earlier about discussions, and I believe I mistakenly referred to discussions on the 3rd of October. I now right -- I now seem to think that -- I was trying to ask you about something on the 3rd of October where I should have asked you about a discussion on the 5th of November. Paragraph 5, did the summer offensive come up in discussions on the 5th of November?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, it did, Your Honours, and General Dimitrijevic quite clearly stated that the Vojska Yugoslavia had, in his opinion, overstepped their rightful course of action during the summer offensive. But in his defence, it was because the Vojska Yugoslavia had to step in in order to salvage what the MUP could not tactically handle. And I think that's a fair comment. He also indicated, just before it in paragraph 4, that General Pavkovic, the 3rd Army commander, may well react without permission from the General Staff, indicating there had been a further, if you will, breakdown and the chain of command was no longer through the normal chief of defence staff but extant from the Supreme Defence Council, or what would be called the Supreme Defence Council, direct to General Pavkovic in Pristina/Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Colonel, what was the "DA" abbreviation of in paragraph 5? "Comment: VJ were quite clearly observed by DA."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DA, Your Honour, is defence attache.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And does that mean you in this case or someone else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: That means myself. And there is also another mistake. MRS is multi-rocket launcher systems MRLS. These are 122-millimetre rocket systems that are extremely destructive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So it looks like "Mrs." but there's an 'L' missing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I beg your pardon. There is an 'L' missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And that's a military expression for --

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: Multi-rocket launcher system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. It had escaped me. Thank you. One final question, if I may, sir, and I may have -- I may have led you on an incorrect date. Perhaps you could clarify this for me: I asked you whether in October Perisic was replaced by Ojdanic. Do you know whether that was in October or November, or do you know the exact date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND
utterances.text: I think, Your Honours, it was during -- during the October period.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Those are my questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have less than 20 minutes left until the close of business today. Could you please tell me how much time I'm going to be allotted for the cross-examination of this witness in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Colonel, you can be back on Monday morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But you want to get away at a reasonable hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be convenient. I have a further meeting on Tuesday, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Milosevic, we anticipate two hours for you for this witness, so there will be 20 minutes, half an hour this afternoon, and you can have a further hour and a half on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But the opposite side had over two hours, as you can see. First of all, one and a half hours, and 35 minutes in this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think your mathematics are out. It was one hour to start with, I don't know about the second session. But let's go on. Let's go on. Let's see how we get on. The witness can come back on Monday morning, but he has to get away.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
